clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive disorder of the RS1 gene (retinoschisin); males are affected and carriers are usually unaffected.
Typically presents in school-age boys with reduced central vision.
Foveal schisis produces a cystic, spoke-wheel (cartwheel) maculopathy.
Peripheral retinoschisis, usually inferotemporal, occurs in a subset of patients.
The electroretinogram is characteristically electronegative, with a reduced b-wave and relatively preserved a-wave.
Optical coherence tomography shows splitting of the inner retinal layers.
Foveal schisis does not leak on fluorescein angiography, which helps distinguish it from cystoid macular oedema.
Vitreous haemorrhage and retinal detachment are the main sight-threatening complications.
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked juvenile retinoschisis is caused by mutations in RS1 on the short arm of the X chromosome, which encodes retinoschisin, a secreted adhesion protein produced by photoreceptors and bipolar cells that maintains the structural integrity and cell-to-cell adhesion of the retina. Loss of functional retinoschisin causes splitting (schisis) within the inner retinal layers, classically producing cystic cavities at the fovea in a radial spoke-wheel pattern and, in a proportion of patients, peripheral (typically inferotemporal) retinoschisis. Because inheritance is X-linked recessive, males are affected while female carriers are generally asymptomatic. Disruption of the photoreceptor-to-bipolar synapse and of Müller cell function impairs transmission of the visual signal, reflected in the characteristic electronegative electroretinogram, a selectively reduced b-wave with relative preservation of the a-wave. Schisis and the associated vitreous changes predispose to vitreous haemorrhage and retinal detachment.
additionalDifferentials: Cystoid macular oedema, which leaks on angiography unlike foveal schisis
Goldmann-Favre syndrome and enhanced S-cone syndrome (NR2E3)
Stargardt disease and other macular dystrophies
Amblyopia and other causes of childhood visual impairment
additionalInvestigations: Optical coherence tomography demonstrating foveal and inner-retinal schisis cavities
Full-field electroretinography showing the electronegative waveform
Fluorescein angiography, characteristically non-leaking in foveal schisis
Dilated fundus examination for spoke-wheel maculopathy and peripheral schisis
B-scan ultrasonography if vitreous haemorrhage obscures the fundus
Examination and carrier testing of family members
redFlags: Sudden loss of vision from vitreous haemorrhage or retinal detachment
A sudden increase in visual field loss
Signs of retinal detachment on examination
reference.prognosis: Vision is usually reduced but relatively stable for years, although foveal atrophy may erode acuity in later life. The visual outlook is considerably worse when disease is complicated by vitreous haemorrhage or retinal detachment.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing foveal schisis as cystoid macular oedema and treating inappropriately; angiography is non-leaking in schisis
Overlooking the diagnostic significance of the electronegative electroretinogram
Attributing a boy's poor vision to amblyopia and missing the maculopathy
Failing to counsel on the contact-sport and head-trauma risk of haemorrhage and detachment
management: A trial of carbonic anhydrase inhibitor therapy, topical or oral, which may reduce foveal schisis cavities as the principal pharmacological option
Low-vision aids and educational support for reduced central acuity
Advice to avoid contact and high-impact sports given the risk of vitreous haemorrhage and retinal detachment
Prompt vitreoretinal surgery for complicating retinal detachment or non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage
Regular monitoring with optical coherence tomography and dilated fundus examination to track macular and peripheral schisis
Refractive correction and amblyopia management in affected children
Genetic counselling with RS1 testing and carrier assessment of female relatives
